title: The False Politics of Western Declinism
gist: Dalgaard and Medish argue Western leaders' declinist rhetoric is factually wrong — their societies keep getting richer — and that conflating lost relative power with falling living standards hands populists a path to convert domestic grievance into nationalist resentment, with Trump's trade war against Canada as the live example.

insights.claim: Political leaders on both sides of the Atlantic increasingly portray the West as declining even as their societies grow richer, making the decline narrative a political construction rather than an economic fact.
insights.speaker: Carl Johan Dalgaard
insights.so_what: If Western decline is rhetoric rather than reality, assets priced for structural Western decay are mispriced — but the politics driving policy risk are real.
insights.quote: Political leaders on both sides of the Atlantic increasingly portray the West as being in decline, even as their societies grow richer.
insights.locator: Political leaders on both sides of the Atlantic

insights.claim: Conflating a loss of relative economic power with a fall in absolute living standards is the specific rhetorical move that gives populists an opening to convert domestic grievances into nationalist resentment.
insights.speaker: Carl Johan Dalgaard
insights.so_what: A usable lens for pricing political risk: watch for relative-vs-absolute framing in leaders' language as a leading indicator of protectionist policy.
insights.quote: By conflating a loss of relative economic power with falling living standards, they give populists an opening to turn domestic grievances into nationalist resentment.
insights.locator: By conflating a loss of relative economic power

insights.claim: The United States, the main architect and beneficiary of the multilateral trading system since 1945, has rhetorically recast itself as the victim of an unfair economic order under Trump.
insights.speaker: Carl Johan Dalgaard
insights.so_what: Signals that US trade policy is now driven by a victim narrative, so further tariff escalation should be treated as the base case rather than the tail.
insights.quote: Despite being the main architect and beneficiary of the multilateral trading system since 1945, the US under Trump has recast itself—at least rhetorically—as the victim of an allegedly unfair economic order.
insights.locator: Despite being the main architect and beneficiary

insights.claim: Trump has opened a trade war against Canada, one of the largest US trading partners and a NATO ally, extending the conflict from rivals to allies.
insights.speaker: Carl Johan Dalgaard
insights.so_what: Ally-directed tariffs raise supply-chain and cross-border earnings risk for North American industrials and energy, and erode the security-economics linkage NATO relies on.
insights.quote: this time with neighboring Canada, one of its largest trading partners, and a NATO ally
insights.locator: As President Donald Trump plunges the United States into another reckless trade war
